title: Miller Effect and Poles
intro: Every real amplifier has capacitances. The Miller effect explains why a small bridging capacitor can dominate the frequency response.

blocks.text: A capacitor CF between the input and output of an amplifier with voltage gain Av = Vout/Vin looks, from the input side, like a capacitor CF*(1 - Av) to ground, and from the output side like CF*(1 - 1/Av) to ground. For an inverting stage (Av is about -20) a 10 fF bridging capacitor appears as 210 fF at the input.
Miller's theorem is exact only for the frequency at which Av is evaluated, so it is an estimate in a frequency-dependent amplifier. It gives a good approximation of the input pole.

A faster rule of thumb: each node with a total capacitance C and a resistance R to ground contributes a pole at 1/(R*C). Write down the nodes, find the equivalent R and C at each (using Miller's theorem for bridging capacitors), and the product gives the pole frequencies. The lowest is the dominant pole.

blocks.title: Miller capacitance
blocks.text: CF = 10 fF bridges a stage with gain -20. Find the capacitance seen from the input and from the output.
blocks.answer: 210 fF at the input and 10.5 fF at the output.
